1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nd2 c5.name: French Defence: Tarrasch Variation, Open System

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nd2 c5 4.exd5.strategy: Settles the tension in the centre at once and leaves Black to choose the recapture. Taking with the pawn frees the light-squared bishop but leaves an isolated queen's pawn; taking with the queen gives Black the healthier structure but lets White's pieces harass it. Either way the game opens and White aims for a lead in development.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nd2 c5 4.Ngf3.strategy: Keeps the tension and defends d4 with a piece, so that a capture on d4 can be answered by recapturing with the knight. White can still decide later whether to take on d5, which often steers the game back into the main lines, though Black can also pick paths that avoid them.
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nd2 c5 4.Ngf3.name: French Defence: Tarrasch Variation, Open System, Euwe-Keres Line
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nd2 c5 4.Ngf3.background: Played by Paul Keres and Max Euwe, and still in significant use.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nd2 c5 4.c3.strategy: Defends d4 with a pawn, but unlike in the closed lines the e4 pawn is still there to be taken. Black releases the tension in the centre and White is left with an isolated queen's pawn that is hard to keep protected. It gives White no advantage.
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nd2 c5 4.c3.name: French Defence: Tarrasch Variation, Open System, Süchting Line

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nd2 c5 4.exd5 Qxd5.strategy: Recaptures with the queen, which White cannot chase away with Nc3 because the b1-knight has already gone to d2. Black intends to win the d4 pawn and swap his c- and d-pawns for White's d- and e-pawns, ending with an extra central pawn; in return White gains time for development by attacking the queen.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nd2 c5 4.exd5 exd5.strategy: Recaptures with the pawn: the light-squared bishop is freed and the centre opens, at the price of an isolated queen's pawn. If White neutralises the activity of Black's pieces in the middlegame, that pawn becomes a target in the ending, so Black has to play for active pieces.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nd2 c5 4.exd5 Nf6.strategy: A gambit: Black develops with an attack on the pawn on d5 instead of recapturing, so White is a pawn up for the moment. Nothing guards that pawn yet, so White has to be careful, but Black must show that quicker development is worth a whole pawn, and the move gives White the easier game.
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nd2 c5 4.exd5 Nf6.name: French Defence: Tarrasch Variation, Open System, Shaposhnikov Gambit
